hn.fm, a year on: Hacker News as episodes, digests, a radio station and directed video

This page is written by Claude, the AI agent that did the November 2026 work on hn.fm, for Brian to read on his own site. It is a draft. Everything you can play on this page was made by the application on 13 November 2026 from stories that were on Hacker News that day. Nothing was edited by hand.
describes a hackathon project: pick a Hacker News story, and a language model, a speech model and an image model turn it into a short narrated video. That was September 2025, on one PC.
The project did not stop there. It now reads every story that reaches Hacker News, decides which are worth making something from, and makes four kinds of thing:
: a two-host conversation about one story, as audio or as an illustrated video.
: a written edition of the day, laid out for an e-reader.
: six shows a day, with hosts, callers, jingles and a song of the hour.
: motion graphics timed to the narration, with each scene chosen by an AI agent. This is the newest part.
Each section below has one of them to play. This is the newest kind, a story video about a claim that was on the front page that morning with 179 points:
story video · 3 min 34 s · made in 5 minutes
DeepSeek and Blackwell: The Hidden Fingerprint
Every scene was chosen by an agent and checked by code. The title, the narration and the figures on screen all come from the story.
What it reads, and what it throws away

Hacker News gets about 800 new submissions a day. Most are not worth a listener's time, and finding that out with a language model on every one would be slow. So the work is ordered from cheap to expensive, and most stories stop early.
New submissions every ten minutes, the front page every half hour.
The linked page is fetched and turned into text. A page with too little text to say anything about stops here, before any model is called.

One model call gives the story two marks: how interesting it is, and how well it can be produced (is there enough in the page to fill three minutes?). The marks become a verdict: great, good, marginal or unsuitable.
The stories worth making get a brief: the thesis, the facts, the numbers, and what the comment thread added that the article did not say.
Everything made later is written from the brief, not from the page. That is why one story can become an episode, a paragraph in the digest and a segment on the radio without being read three times.
Since the database was started in September the numbers look like this:
On the day this page was made, 827 stories came in, 744 were scored and 294 of those were good or great.
An episode is the original idea, grown up. From the brief, the model writes a script for two hosts in short sections. Then:
Each section is spoken by a text-to-speech model, one voice per host.

A speech recogniser transcribes the result. This gives the exact second each word is spoken, which is what the captions are timed from. It is also a check: if what was heard is far from what was written, the take is flagged.
For the video form, the model writes an image prompt for each section and an image model draws it, then draws four variations so the picture changes while the hosts talk.
ffmpeg cuts the pictures to the audio, with captions and a title card.
Every step is recorded with its inputs, its output, how long it took and which prompt version it used. Any step can be opened and run again by itself.

The illustrated episode has a weakness. The pictures are atmosphere. When a host says "64 GB", the screen shows a moody drawing of a circuit board.
The story video is a different way to fill the screen. It is built with

, which renders a web page to video: the page is HTML, the motion is a GSAP timeline, and a headless browser steps through it frame by frame. So a scene can be a number that counts up, two things side by side, a bar chart, or a line of text that arrives as it is spoken.
Someone has to decide which of those each scene should be. That job goes to
, an AI agent that already runs on the home cluster.
The first attempt, and why it failed

The first version asked the agent to write each scene's HTML and animation, working from a skill that explained the rules and showed one worked example. The local model returned the worked example. For a line about 64 GB of memory it produced a scene that said "24 GB", a number that appears nowhere in the story.

This is the same lesson the radio station taught earlier in the month. A small local model is good at choosing and at phrasing. It is not reliable at producing a large structure with every detail right.
The work is split so that each side does what it is good at.
It writes the page, the captions, the title card, the sign-off, and a plain version of every scene. A video can always be made, even with the agent switched off.
: a single figure, a comparison, bars, a list, steps, a phrase, a quote, and a picture. Each one is a layout with its motion already written.

For each scene it is sent the line of narration, the numbers the narrator says in it, and what the last few scenes looked like. It replies with a small card: which treatment, and the words to put in it.
language-json shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark monokai
{"treatment": "figure", "value": "64 GB", "label": "unified memory", "why": "the line turns on one number"}
A card is checked before it is used, and sent back with the reason if it fails:
A number on screen must be a number the narrator says in that line.
The words on screen must come from the narration.
A phrase must be a run of consecutive words from the line, and must not end on a word like "the".
Two scenes in a row should not look the same.
The built scene is then opened by the renderer, which reports text that runs off the frame, text hidden under something else, and colours too close to read.
The agent gets three tries per scene. After that the scene keeps its plain version.
Here is what the agent chose for the video at the top of the page, one frame per scene, with the title card first:
One frame from each scene of the story video
All nine scenes were directed. Six of the nine cards were accepted first time. The numbers on screen (1,385 sigma, 461 rows, 469 rows, 49 sigma) are all numbers the narrator says in that scene.
It is not always that tidy. This is the story video for the audio episode above:
story video · 2 min 46 s · 9 of 13 scenes directed
Four scenes kept their plain version, where the screen shows the opening words of the line.
Four of its thirteen scenes were refused three times and kept their plain version. The refusals are in the video's record, and they show the checks doing their job and also being strict:
For a line with no number in it, the agent asked for bars comparing "64 tokens/s" with "10 tokens/s". Neither figure is in the story. Refused, correctly.
For "within an hour", it asked for the figure "1 hour". The narrator says "an hour", not "1". Refused, and a person would have let it through.

For "only about 10 billion of the 145 billion parameters", it asked for bars labelled "active params" and "total params". Refused because "active" and "total" are not words in the narration, although the chart would have been right.
A plain scene is a dull scene, not a wrong one. That is the trade the checks make. It is also not a fixed result. The same video made again an hour later had all thirteen scenes directed.
Across the first three videos made that day, 30 of 35 scenes were directed. A video takes about five minutes: one minute of directing and four of rendering.
Keeping the agent in a small room

What the agent reads is written from web pages by strangers. An agent with tools could, in principle, be talked into using them. So hn.fm does not talk to the main Hermes agent. It talks to a second profile of its own with these properties:
It cannot run a command, read a file or open a page. It can only answer.
That key works on that profile and nowhere else, and the main agent's key does not work on it.
It does not think out loud.
With the model's reasoning mode on, one card took three minutes. With it off, four seconds.
Its instructions travel with each request.
The skill is a file in the hn.fm repository and is sent along every time. When the model was instead given a tool for reading skills, it spent its turns trying to save its answer as a new skill.
The same skill is also installed in Hermes itself, so the agent can be asked for a card by hand.

The digest is the quiet part of the project and the one Brian reads most. Each morning it takes the best-scored stories of the last day and writes an edition: a lead, a set of short items, two longer pieces and something odd at the end. It is rendered as a single HTML file sized for an e-reader and sent there by email.

There are four shapes of edition, which differ in how the same stories are written up: a daily, a scan (many stories, two lines each), a punchline (one sentence each) and a narrative (the day told as one piece). An edition gets a name and a cover from the image model.
This is the top of an edition made from the day's stories. The model named it "Silicon Redlining" and the image model drew the cover and the illustrations. It was not sent anywhere.
The top of a digest: a cover, the edition's name, a lead paragraph and the first story

The lead paragraph shows the model's habit when asked to tie ten stories together: it merges them. Nobody ran a language model on a 1994 Jeep's engine computer. One story was about models on old devices, and another was about two coding agents working out how a Jeep's engine computer works. The items underneath, each written from one brief, do not have this problem.

Making this edition also turned up a fault. Asked for the last day's stories, the first attempt came back full of stories from September. The check on a story's date compared a date with a piece of text, so it never rejected anything. It had gone unnoticed because the scheduled editions do not ask for a window at all.
The station is covered at length in
, so this is the short version.
The shape of the hour is code.
Six shows cover the day. Each has two hosts, a tone, its own music and a clock: four quarters, each an ordered list of slots such as headline, two-hander, phone-in, bulletin and song of the hour.
The model is asked one question per block
: which story goes in which slot.
writes each piece from the story's fact sheet, checks it against rules, has an editor prompt read it, and rewrites once.
speaks every line, transcribes it back and compares it with the script. A line that came out wrong is spoken again. Callers are put down a telephone line. Music is ducked under speech.
With no listener the station plays music from its library and leaves the models alone.

The models, and checking that they answer
Every model runs on machines in Brian's home network and is reached over HTTP. Nothing on this page was made by a paid API.

Ten services is a lot to depend on, and the project's worst failure this year was a quiet one: the writing model's address stopped answering and every call failed for weeks without anything saying so. There is now a check that sends one real request to each model, with a time limit on each so that one that hangs cannot hold up the rest.
The desk's panel of models, each with the result of its last check
On the day this page was made, eight of the ten answered:

Two steps ask a model to look at a picture: reading the images found in an article, and planning the picture sequence of an episode. No model that can read pictures is running at the moment, so both steps fail. The application carries on without them, but this is the one real gap.
The video-clip model is switched off on purpose.
It needs a whole graphics card to itself.
The 2025 version was Docker Compose on one PC. It is now a Helm chart on a home Kubernetes cluster:
An API and four kinds of worker
, one each for fetching, scoring, rendering and digests, so a slow render never holds up the front page.
Postgres, Redis and an S3-compatible object store
for HyperFrames: Node, Chromium and ffmpeg behind a small HTTP server.
A push builds the images on a self-hosted Forgejo, and Argo CD rolls them out. A change is live about ten minutes after the push.
Everything is run from one page, the desk, which shows what was last made of each kind, a button to make the next one, and the switch for each.
The desk: something to read, something to hear, something to watch
What went wrong along the way
The renderer updated itself in the middle of a render.

The HyperFrames command-line tool installs a newer version of itself the first time it runs. It did this while it was rendering, replacing its own files. The version is now pinned and the update check is off.
The writing model froze for a day.
It was still running and still accepted connections, but never replied. The inference check waited on it for 25 minutes. That is where the per-model time limits came from.
Starting a second agent took the first one offline.

While setting up the Hermes profile, a command that looked like "start this profile" took over the port the main agent was serving on. It was down for three minutes. The setup script now carries a warning at the top.
The same video was made twice at once.
A job delivered twice had two workers rewriting one project. A video that is already being made is now refused.
fetching, scoring, research, episodes as audio and as video, digests, the radio station, story videos, and the check of every model.
the schedule that makes digests and episodes by itself, and the radio's own production. Fetching and scoring run all day. Everything else is made when asked for.
anything that needs a model to look at a picture.

the eight treatments cover numbers and short phrases well. They have nothing for a line that is an argument with no figure in it, which is why the plain scenes in the second video are where they are. More treatments are the obvious next step, and so is a stronger model writing scenes freely, which the code still supports.

A 2025 hackathon project that turned Hacker News stories into narrated video kept growing. This is what it does now, how each part works, and a set of things it made from one day's front page, all on models running at home.
From Pokédex artwork to 3D models: every Pokémon, in clay, glass and chrome

This page is written by Claude, the AI agent that did the 2026 half of this work, for Brian to read on his own site. It is a draft. The 2025 half is Brian's, reconstructed from the files he left behind. Every 3D model on this page is real output and can be turned by dragging it.

The picture at the top of this page is the whole project in one frame. On the wall is a flat drawing of Pikachu from the Pokédex. On the plinths are eight 3D models that were generated from it, each in a different material. Nobody sculpted any of them.
Here is the same set, live. Pick a material. The left pane is the picture that went into the 3D model and the right pane is the model that came out.
The Pokédex is a good test set for image-to-3D models:
There are 1,025 Pokémon, each with one official drawing on a plain background.
There are round ones, spiky ones, ones made of chains or keys or ice cream, and ones with wings as thin as paper.
You do not need a benchmark to see that Charizard's wings are wrong.
Each entry has a height, a weight, types, stats and an evolution line, so the models can be scaled and grouped without anyone typing anything.
The pipeline has three steps, and the middle one is optional:
the drawing and the data for each Pokémon.
the drawing with an image-editing model, so the flat cartoon becomes a picture of a physical object.
it: give the picture to an image-to-3D model and get a textured mesh back.
Brian built the first version in late August and early September 2025, on a single desktop PC with an RTX 4090. It was never a repository. It was a folder of Python scripts next to 26 GB of output.
A Playwright script walked the official Pokédex and saved 1,025 drawings, plus one YAML file per Pokémon with its types, height, weight, stats, description and evolutions.
Each drawing went through FLUX.1 Kontext in InvokeAI with a six-word prompt:

. This turns line art into something that looks like a rendered toy, which gives the 3D model shading to work from. The README carries a list of about 470 Pokédex numbers under the heading "Redo InvokeAI", so a lot of them needed a second attempt.
The restyled pictures went one at a time through a Hunyuan3D 2.1 workflow in ComfyUI. Each model has 200,000 faces and weighs about 6 MB. It finished 1,017 of the 1,025. Eight never got a model.
A Blender script stood each model on the ground and scaled it to its true height from the Pokédex. 935 were processed.

Then the project wandered, in the way good side projects do. There is a script that measures the volume of every mesh, a set of charts of height against weight, an attempt to pack all thousand footprints into the smallest possible circle with NVIDIA's cuOpt solver, a Blender file with the first hundred laid out in a grid, and a small web page for trying the TRELLIS model as an alternative. The last file was touched on 14 September 2025.
These are 42 of those 2025 models, rendered straight from the files:
A contact sheet of 42 Pokémon models generated in 2025
Most are very good. Some are not: Ivysaur came out attached to a grey backing plate, and thin shapes such as Onix and Lugia broke apart. Here are six of the good ones to turn.

The brief this time was short: find the project, finish it, and add the material step. The folder turned up in a salvage directory on a machine in Brian's home cluster. The outputs were all there. What was missing was everything around them:
There was no way to look at the results. Checking a model meant opening a file.
There was no record of which ones were bad, apart from that list of numbers in a README.
A retry meant editing a script and running it again.
The image and 3D models it called were desktop applications that are no longer running.
The home cluster now serves both kinds of model behind one gateway, so the new version does not run any models itself. It sends a picture and gets a picture or a mesh back:
FLUX.3 Klein, about 10 seconds a picture
TRELLIS.2, about 40 to 65 seconds a model

The 2025 restyle had one job: make the drawing look three-dimensional. The new one asks for a material. Every prompt has the same second half, which is there to stop the image model from redrawing the character:
Re-render this character as a handmade stop-motion claymation figure sculpted from matte modeling clay, with visible fingerprints and soft tool marks.
Keep the same character, pose, silhouette and proportions. Single full-body figure, centered, plain white background, soft even studio lighting, no text.
There are eight materials so far: clay, stained glass, carved wood, origami, chrome, crochet, bronze and toy bricks. A style is a name and a prompt, and adding one adds a column to the studio.
The 3D model then has to turn a picture of a material into geometry. Things to look for in the viewer at the top of the page:
whether the stitches became bumps in the mesh or stayed as paint.
whether the folds became flat facets with hard creases.
the lead lines survive as dark seams, but the model is solid. Nothing in this pipeline can make a mesh transparent.
a picture of a mirror is mostly a picture of its surroundings, and the 3D model paints those reflections onto the surface as if they were colour.

Restyled by FLUX.3 Klein from the Pokédex artwork. The seed for a first attempt is the Pokédex number, so a first attempt can be repeated.

The 2025 models came from Hunyuan3D 2.1 and were built from the restyled picture. The 2026 models below come from TRELLIS.2 and were built from the flat drawing with no restyle at all. So this is not a clean comparison of two models, because the inputs differ too. It is a comparison of two pipelines.
Until each model loads, its stage shows the picture it was made from: a shaded render on the left, a flat drawing on the right.

Neither pipeline is clean. Working from the flat drawing, TRELLIS.2 gave Gengar a dark slab on one side, and it added something extra beside Charizard's tail flame. These are first attempts with no retries, which is what the studio is for.

The part that was missing in 2025 is the part that took the most work: a place to see everything, choose, and try again. It is a FastAPI application with a SQLite database and a page that needs no build step.
The main view is a grid. Each row is a Pokémon and each column is a style. A cell shows the picture, and a badge says whether it has a model, is queued, is running, or failed.
The studio's grid: Pokémon in rows, styles in columns
Opening a Pokémon shows every version side by side, picture above model, with the models turning together:
One Pokémon's page: each style with its picture, its model and its controls
From here each cell can be:
approved, marked as needing a fix, or rejected
with a new seed or an edited prompt for that one Pokémon;
kept as several attempts, with one
Generating a thousand of anything means some will fail, so the queue is built around failure:
There are three stages (restyle, model, video), each with its own worker, so a slow 3D job never blocks a fast image job.
A model job waits for its restyle job. If the restyle fails, the model job does not run.
A job is tried up to three times, with a pause between attempts.
Three failures in a row pause the whole stage and put the reason at the top of every page. This stops a broken service from burning through a thousand queued jobs.
Everything is in the database, so a restart loses nothing.

That last safeguard went off while this article was being written, and the screenshot below is real. The toy-brick Pikachu failed three times inside the 3D service with a GPU error. After that the service was holding all of the graphics card's memory, every job behind it failed with "out of memory", and the stage paused itself with seven models still waiting. They are still waiting. That is why this page has a toy-brick picture and no toy-brick model.
The queue after the model stage paused itself
A film set for the models

A model on a grey background is hard to get excited about, so the studio also makes short films. Each one is a Three.js scene: a habitat chosen from the Pokémon's type (a meadow for grass types, a lava field for fire, a shore for water), with the model standing in it.

The films are rendered by HyperFrames, which turns a web page into video by stepping through it one frame at a time. That only works if the page can draw any frame on request, in any order. So the scene has no animation loop and no clock. It has one function that takes a time and draws the picture for that time. In outline:

Getting 20 MB models onto a web page
The models on this page are not the files the generators made. Those are 6 to 22 MB each, and this page has 21 of them. Each one here is about 0.4 MB.

The usual way to shrink a mesh is to simplify it and keep the texture. That did not work on the TRELLIS.2 models. Their textures are cut into a very large number of tiny islands, and a simplifier will not merge triangles across the edge of an island. Asking for 60,000 faces gave back 210,000.
Bake the texture into the vertices.
Look up the colour under every vertex and store it on the vertex. The texture is no longer needed.
Without texture coordinates, the copies of a vertex along every island edge become one vertex.
to 80,000 faces, with colour counted as part of the error so that eyes and outlines keep their vertices.

The cost is fine detail in the painted surface, which now has one colour per vertex where it had one per texel. Both generators' models went through the same steps, so the comparisons above are like for like. The films and the cover use the full-size files.
Reading a year-old project's output with new code turned up a few things:
They carry a metallic value that makes them shine like gold in a physically based renderer. It is removed, except for the two metal styles.
Their vertices are split along triangle edges, so the normals cannot be smoothed until the mesh is welded.
The bounds stored in the files are wrong, so anything that trusted them stood the model above the ground. The bounds are now measured from the geometry.

A 2025 side project turned 1,017 flat Pokédex drawings into 3D models and then sat on a hard drive. This is how it worked, what it took to bring it back, and what a restyle step, a review studio and a virtual film set add to it.
Reviving old projects with AI: the working log

This page is written by Claude, the AI agent doing the work, as a log for Brian to read on the site itself. It is a draft and will become source material for an article in his own words. Newest entries are at the top of the log; the first sections are kept current.

Every stylesheet on this site names Montserrat, but nothing loaded it, so visitors saw Arial or Helvetica. The design-system pull request loads it. That changes how every page looks, so it is not merged. It is one commit and can be dropped on its own.

The radio station now sings its own jingles and one short song an hour. Speech is checked automatically before it airs; singing cannot be. Someone has to listen and say whether the jingles are usable.

The video model's server is stopped, and it lives on the same machine as the registry, the git server and the deploy controller. Starting a 22-billion-parameter model there was not a decision to take alone. Show idents and song clips are designed and not built.
The public repository is far behind the code the cluster runs. Issues are tracked on the public side. Nothing was pushed there.
A release pull request (version 1.1.0 of this site) is open and can be merged whenever the changelog should be cut.
Story fetching is running again. The switch that sends the daily digests to the e-reader and makes videos on a schedule is still off. It is one switch on the schedule page.
hn.fm: what was found and what was done

The article on this site describes a hackathon project from September 2025: Hacker News stories turned into narrated video by a language model, a speech model and an image model on one PC. The project kept growing after the article. By this autumn it had a Postgres database, a triage step that scores stories, a daily digest sent to an e-reader, a Helm chart, a build pipeline, and the beginnings of an internet radio station.
The deployed copy had been failing quietly.

Its text model route no longer answered and had no fallback, so every model call on the cluster returned an error. The image service it pointed at had been replaced by a newer one under a different name. Nothing on its status page said so.
The radio had never run on the cluster.
It worked on a laptop. The chart's radio templates had never been rendered with the switch on.
One prompt had never worked as written.
The prompt for the station's short comedy bits put its style guide in a part of the file that is sent as-is, so the model received the literal text

The old station asked a model to invent thirty minutes of programming, then ran 170 lines of code to repair what came back. The rebuild swaps the jobs. Code owns the shape of the hour; the model owns the choices inside it.
, each with two hosts, a tone and its own music: Cold Start, Main Thread, The Diff, Show and Tell, Night Shift, Garbage Collection.
for each show: four quarters, each an ordered list of slots. A slot is a segment type.

, among them a two-hander, a phone-in where callers voice points from the comment thread down a telephone line, a top-of-the-hour bulletin, the front page read as a weather forecast, a mock sponsor read, and a song of the hour.
One question for the model per block
: which story goes in which slot. Anything it returns that does not fit is replaced by rule.
: a fact sheet per story, a draft, rule checks, an editor prompt, one rewrite, and a final pass that cuts any sentence the rules still reject.
: every spoken line is transcribed by a speech recogniser and compared with its script. A line that came out wrong is spoken again.
: with no listener the station plays music from its library and leaves the models alone. Someone tuning in wakes it. Three scheduled editions a day keep the archive growing.
: each finished block is kept as one file, with a podcast feed.
Measured on the home cluster, per block of five to nine minutes of air:
19,000 to 47,000, mostly an unchanging system prompt
Once it was deployed, the station was asked for a block of every quarter of every show, one at a time. It made 24. Nineteen had enough speech to keep.
24 minutes, spread over about an hour
They are on the station's listen page under "Listen again", and in its podcast feed.
The second pass: fewer things, made better

Brian's direction after hearing the station was to stop making radio around the clock and put the effort into the quality of what is made and into running the project from one place. Production was switched off the same hour. What followed:

Twelve effects are synthesised from sine waves and noise by ffmpeg, with no recordings: the pips before the bulletin, a ring and a click before a caller, static around a correspondent, a whoosh and a low hit around the announcer. Six treatments say where a voice is speaking from: the studio, a phone, a line from outside, the announcer's big voice, fine print read fast at the end of an advert. Segments name their effects in code. The model never chooses a sound.

Measuring the speech model showed every mood is a different voice (calm runs 40 to 90 per cent slower; only one host can sound happy, only two fearful) and that four speakers the station never used can be understood in English. There are now six hosts, three correspondents, an announcer and twelve caller voices.
A cold open cut from the opening lines of the pieces that follow it, with no model call. The front page as a countdown. A report from a correspondent.

A whole hour of a show is made as one programme with chapter marks, a transcript, cover art drawn by the image model, a page where the line being spoken is lit, and a video. The first, an hour of the morning show: 32 of 32 items, 21 minutes 38 seconds, made in about five minutes, speech matching its script at 0.96.
One page with a column each for reading, radio and video: what was last made, a button to make the next, and its switch. Radio production is now a setting, not a deploy.

Two findings from this pass belong with the ones below. Given a paragraph describing a host's character, the model read it out as copy; of a story about a teacher assaulted by a student it wrote that the host "counts that among the small clever things that delight her". Character sheets are now two lines about manner, and any sentence sharing four words with one is cut. And asked to stop borrowing from the worked example, the model more than once handed back the example itself; the borrowed sentence is now cut by rule and the earlier draft kept. On the same twelve stories as before: none failed (one had), all twelve passed the rules (eleven had), eleven passed the editor (ten had).

What is still not good, from reading that first episode: headlines that are a list of facts with no shape, one that made no sense, callers who introduce themselves as members of a demographic, and a two-host conversation that ran thirteen turns (now held to eight). The structure and the sound are the station's; the sentences are the local model's, and it shows.
The text model is fast and small. It answers in about a second. Four things about it shaped the design more than any plan did.
Told to "open on the hook", it wrote "The hook: seven years of updates." Labels in the input were read out too. The input now has no labels, and a rule cuts any sentence that recites.
It cannot be told to think a little.

With thinking on it produced four thousand tokens of reasoning and no answer, whatever budget was requested. Everything runs with thinking off. The writer fills in three short fields first (the hook, the facts, the ending) and then writes, which is thinking at a fixed price.
It follows an example and ignores a rule.
Each segment type has one worked example. A test holds the examples to the station's own rules, because an example that breaks a rule teaches the opposite.
It copies whatever it is shown.

Given the research brief, it read the brief back. Given the earlier items in the block for continuity, it lifted whole sentences from them into unrelated stories. It is now shown only a short fact sheet for the story in hand.
Its editor prompt is the weak part. It scores nearly everything five out of five. The rules written in code are what hold quality.
Was it better? A measured answer

The same twelve stories were written twice: once by the old prompt (the title, then three bullet points read aloud) and once by the rebuilt writers' room. Both sets went through the same rule checks and the same editor.
Mean length (the slot wants about 70 words)
Pieces with nothing for the rules to object to
Pieces where nothing usable was written

Then a stronger model read the twelve pairs as a listener, without being told which was which. It preferred the new piece in seven pairs and the old in three, with two ties. That reading is not fully blind, because a piece that opens on its own title is recognisably the old format.

The more useful result was what the reading found. Four defects in the new pipeline showed up in those twelve pairs, and each was fixed the same hour with a test: a sentence cut in the middle of a spelled-out acronym, invented callers, "10th" read as "ten th", and notes about "the source" read on air. A second read of the two weakest segment types found four more. Measuring was worth more than the score.

So the honest summary is: clearly better, not ten times better, at two and a half times the model time per piece. The gains that are closer to tenfold are structural. The station costs nothing when nobody listens. A wrong word no longer reaches the air unheard. A new segment type is one entry in one file.

One header for every width, a menu that works with a keyboard, and pickers for language and colour mode that announce their state.

Everything so far was done by one model, Claude Fable 5.2, working in a terminal session with access to the repositories and read access to the cluster. The comparison Brian asked for, the same tasks handed to a local model through Hermes, has not been run yet. The radio work is a preview of what it will show: the local model is a capable writer inside a tight structure and an unreliable judge of its own work.

hn.fm story videos: a narrated story is now one HyperFrames composition, and the Hermes agent directs it. For each scene the agent returns a small card (a figure, a comparison, bars, a list, a phrase and so on), code checks the card against the narration and builds the scene. The agent works from a profile with no tools and its own key.
A check of every model on the desk. Eight of ten answer. No model that can read pictures is running, which is the one real gap; the video-clip model is stopped on purpose.

One of each kind of output made from the day's stories: an illustrated episode, an audio episode, a digest (not sent), a radio block and three story videos. All were made. Doing it turned up five faults, now fixed, among them a digest of "the last day" that was filled with stories from September.
A draft article about hn.fm as it is now, with that day's output to play, is on its own pull request.
The cluster's writing model had stopped answering for a day and was restarted.
